title: Noun Genders and Declension Groups
subtitle: Determine masculine and feminine declension groups by nominative endings
keyPoint: Every Latvian noun is either masculine (typically ending in -s, -š, or -is) or feminine (typically ending in -a, -e, or rarely -s).

mistakes.note: 'Galds' ends in -s and is masculine, so it requires masculine adjectives like 'liels'.
'Puķe' ends in -e and is a 5th declension feminine noun, requiring feminine agreement.
Although ending in -s, 'suns' (dog) is a 2nd declension masculine noun.

quiz.question: Which of the following nouns belongs to the 1st declension (masculine)?
quiz.explanation: 'Tēvs' ends in -s, making it a classic 1st declension masculine noun.

quiz.question: The noun 'zeme' (earth, land) belongs to which declension group?
quiz.explanation: Feminine nouns ending in -e belong to the 5th declension.

quiz.question: Which word is a 3rd declension masculine noun?
quiz.explanation: Nouns ending in -us such as 'tirgus' belong to the 3rd declension.

quiz.question: Identify the 4th declension feminine noun from the list:
quiz.explanation: Nouns ending in -a like 'grāmata' belong to the 4th declension.

tip: Almost every noun ending in -a or -e is feminine, while almost every noun ending in -s, -š, or -is is masculine.

title: Three Verb Conjugation Classes in Present Tense
subtitle: Conjugate short, long, and mixed verbs in the present tense
keyPoint: Latvian verbs fall into three conjugations based on their stem changes and present-tense suffixes.

mistakes.note: 'Lasīt' is a 3rd conjugation verb; its present 1st person form is 'lasu', not 'lasīju' (which is past).
Drop the infinitive ending -t and use the present ending -ā for 3rd person in the 2nd conjugation.

mistakes.wrong: Mēs gribam iet, bet viņi negribat.
mistakes.right: Mēs gribam iet, bet viņi negrib.
mistakes.note: The 3rd person plural (viņi/viņas) always shares the exact same form as 3rd person singular (viņš/viņa).

quiz.question: Complete with the correct present tense form: 'Es tagad birojā ___ (strādāt).'
quiz.explanation: For 2nd conjugation verbs like 'strādāt', the 1st person singular 'es' takes '-ju', giving 'strādāju'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Viņa katru rītu ___ (dzert) tēju.'
quiz.explanation: The 3rd person singular present of 'dzert' is 'dzer'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct form: 'Mēs ātri ___ (skriet) uz parku.'
quiz.explanation: The 1st person plural pronoun 'mēs' takes the ending '-am', giving 'skrienam'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Ko jūs tagad ___ (darīt)?'
quiz.explanation: 'Darīt' is a 3rd conjugation verb where 'jūs' takes '-āt': 'jūs darāt'.

tip: In Latvian, 3rd person singular (viņš/viņa) and 3rd person plural (viņi/viņas) ALWAYS use the identical verb form.

title: Locative Case for Place and Time
subtitle: Express static locations and specific times without prepositions
keyPoint: The locative case uses lengthened vowels (-ā, -ē, -ī, -ū) without any preposition to indicate 'in', 'at', or 'on'.

cells: on the table / in the park
in the wardrobe / in the brother
at the market / in the ice
in the river / in the kitchen

examples.en: Visi dokumenti stāv uz galda vai plauktā.
Svētdienā mēs parasti braucam uz laukiem.

mistakes.note: Latvian does not use prepositions like 'iekš' or 'iekšā' for static locations; use the locative suffix -ā instead.
'Virtuve' is 5th declension and takes -ē in the locative singular, not the accusative -i.
Movement toward a destination uses 'uz + accusative', while static position uses the locative 'parkā'.

quiz.question: How do you say 'in the shop' (veikals)?
quiz.explanation: The 1st declension masculine noun 'veikals' forms the locative singular with '-ā': 'veikalā'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Bērni mācās ___ (skola).'
quiz.explanation: The 4th declension feminine noun 'skola' takes the locative singular ending '-ā': 'skolā'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct locative form of 'istaba' (room): 'Kaķis guļ ___.'
quiz.explanation: 'Istaba' becomes 'istabā' in the locative singular.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Pārtika atrodas aukstā ___ (ledusskapis).'
quiz.explanation: 2nd declension nouns ending in -is replace the ending with long '-ī' in the locative: 'ledusskapī'.

tip: To make the locative singular, simply lengthen the final vowel of the nominative ending: -a becomes -ā, -e becomes -ē, -is becomes -ī, and -us becomes -ū.

title: Accusative Case for Direct Objects
subtitle: Form accusative singular and plural nouns when receiving an action
keyPoint: Direct objects of transitive verbs take the accusative case, marked by -u in the singular for nearly all noun declensions.

mistakes.note: 'Kafija' is the direct object of 'gribēt', so it must take the accusative singular ending -u.
Direct objects of transitive verbs cannot remain in the nominative case; use 'grāmatu'.
2nd declension nouns in -is (like 'brālis') drop -is and end in -i in the accusative singular, not -u.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence with the accusative object: 'Tēvs pērk jaunu ___ (auto / mašīna).'
quiz.explanation: 4th declension feminine noun 'mašīna' takes '-u' in accusative singular: 'mašīnu'.

quiz.question: Which form completes the sentence: 'Es redzu tavu ___ (brālis).'?
quiz.explanation: 2nd declension masculine nouns in -is end in '-i' in the accusative singular: 'brāli'.

quiz.question: Select the correct plural direct object: 'Mēs pērkam svaigus ___ (ābols).'?
quiz.explanation: 1st declension masculine nouns take '-us' in the accusative plural: 'ābolus'.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Vai jūs dzerat melnu ___ (tēja)?'
quiz.explanation: 'Tēja' takes '-u' as a singular direct object: 'tēju'.

tip: Almost all singular nouns end in -u in the accusative, except 2nd and 5th declensions (-is, -e), which end in -i.

title: Dative Case and Preposition Government
subtitle: Master indirect objects for recipients and essential dative prepositions
keyPoint: The dative case marks the recipient ('to/for someone') and is required after prepositions like 'līdz' (until), 'pa' (along), and 'pa priekšu' (ahead of).

examples.en: Mēs brauksim ciemos pie vecmāmiņas līdz vakaram.
Ko tu uzdāvināsi brālim dzimšanas dienā?

mistakes.note: The recipient must be in the dative case (-am for 1st declension masculine), not nominative.
The preposition 'līdz' always requires the dative case ('līdz skolai').

mistakes.wrong: Es rakstu vēstuli mātei un tēvei.
mistakes.right: Es rakstu vēstuli mātei un tēvam.
mistakes.note: 'Tēvs' is masculine (1st declension) and takes the dative suffix '-am', not feminine '-ei'.

quiz.question: Which form correctly completes: 'Es saku paldies ___ (māte).'?
quiz.explanation: 5th declension feminine noun 'māte' takes '-ei' in the dative singular: 'mātei'.

quiz.question: Complete the prepositional phrase: 'Mēs ejam līdz ___ (parks).'
quiz.explanation: 'Līdz' governs the dative; 1st declension 'parks' becomes 'parkam'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct recipient: 'Jānis dāvina ziedus savai ___ (draudzene).'
quiz.explanation: 5th declension 'draudzene' takes the dative singular ending '-ei': 'draudzenei'.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank with the plural recipient: 'Skolotāja skaidro uzdevumu ___ (skolēni).'
quiz.explanation: Masculine nouns in the dative plural take '-iem': 'skolēniem'.

tip: Masculine dative singular always ends in '-m' (-am, -im, -um), whereas feminine dative singular always ends in '-i' (-ai, -ei, -ij).

title: Verbal Negation and 'Nav'
subtitle: Form negative verbs with 'ne-' and express absence with 'nav'
keyPoint: Prefix 'ne-' directly to standard verbs, but replace the affirmative copula 'ir' entirely with 'nav'.

cells: I know / I do not know
He is / is not a teacher
I have / don't have a cat

mistakes.note: The negative prefix 'ne-' must be written attached directly to the verb without a space.
Never say 'ne ir'; the present negative form of the verb 'būt' (to be) is always 'nav'.
When expressing the absence of something or negative possession with 'nav', the noun takes the genitive case, not nominative.

quiz.question: How do you say 'I do not work today'?
quiz.explanation: The negative marker 'ne-' is prefixed directly to the inflected verb 'strādāju'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Pēteris šodien ___ skolā.' (Peter is not at school today.)
quiz.explanation: 'Nav' is the invariant third-person negative copula for 'to be'.

quiz.question: Complete the negative sentence: 'Mums nav ___.' (We do not have bread.)
quiz.explanation: Negative existence and possession with 'nav' require the genitive case ('maizes').

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly exhibits Latvian double negation?
quiz.explanation: Latvian requires multiple negative elements: negative adverbs like 'nekad' (never) must co-occur with a negated verb ('nezinu').

tip: Latvian mandates negative concord (double/multiple negatives): words like 'nekad' (never) and 'neviens' (nobody) always require 'ne-' or 'nav' on the main verb.

title: Debitive Mood (Vajadzības izteiksme)
subtitle: Express obligation using 'jā-' prefixed to present stems with dative subjects
keyPoint: Form the debitive by prefixing 'jā-' to the 3rd person present verb stem, changing the logical subject to the dative case.

examples.en: Viņai rīt būs jādodas uz slimnīcu.

mistakes.note: The agent of a debitive construction must be in the dative case ('man'), not the nominative ('es').
The debitive prefix 'jā-' is always affixed to the 3rd person present stem ('mācās'), never to the 1st person form.
In standard modern debitive syntax, regular noun direct objects shift from accusative to the nominative case ('grāmata').

quiz.question: Select the correct sentence for 'I must read this book':
quiz.explanation: The subject takes the dative ('man'), the verb uses the 3rd-person present stem with 'jā-' ('jālasa'), and the direct object becomes nominative ('šī grāmata').

quiz.question: How do you express 'We had to wait' in the past?
quiz.explanation: Past debitive requires dative logical subject ('mums'), past auxiliary 'bija', and the debitive form 'jāgaida'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: '___ rīt agri jāceļas.' (You [singular informal] have to get up early tomorrow.)
quiz.explanation: The logical subject of a debitive verb must appear in the dative case ('tev').

quiz.question: Which verb form correctly completes: 'Viņai šodien ___ mājās.' (She must stay home.)
quiz.explanation: Debitive stems are built exclusively from the 3rd-person present tense ('paliek' -> 'jāpaliek').

tip: Personal pronouns as direct objects in the debitive remain in the accusative (e.g., 'Tev mani jāsaprot' - You must understand me), while regular nouns shift to the nominative.

title: Dative Predicative Possession
subtitle: Express possession via 'dative possessor + ir + nominative object'
keyPoint: Latvian does not use a verb meaning 'to have'; instead, the possessor is in the dative case and the possessed item is the grammatical nominative subject of 'ir'.

cells: He will have a lot of time
We do not have free seats

examples.en: Man ir liels un ērts dzīvoklis.
Vai tev ir šīs pilsētas karte?
Viņai bija gari un gaiši mati.

mistakes.note: Do not translate English 'I have' into nominative 'Es'; the possessor must be dative ('Man').
The possessed object is the grammatical subject of the sentence, so it takes nominative ('suns'), not accusative ('suni').
Quantifiers like 'daudz' (much/many) or 'maz' (few/little) trigger the genitive case ('naudas').

quiz.question: How do you correctly say 'Do you have a question?' in Latvian?
quiz.explanation: The possessor pronoun must be dative ('tev') and the possessed thing nominative ('jautājums').

quiz.question: Fill the blank: '___ rīt būs jauns dators.' (He will have a new computer tomorrow.)
quiz.explanation: 'Viņam' is the masculine singular 3rd person dative pronoun required by the possession pattern.

quiz.question: Choose the correct past-tense possession sentence:
quiz.explanation: 'Man bija' sets the past possession, and 'daudz' demands the genitive case 'darba'.

quiz.question: What is the grammatical case of 'suns' in 'Mums ir liels suns'?
quiz.explanation: The possessed item functions as the syntactic grammatical subject of the copula 'ir', thus taking the nominative case.

tip: Remember that 'ir' acts like an equals sign: [To me] = [a dog]. Since the item itself 'is' there, it stands in the nominative case!

title: Consonant Mutation (Līdzskaņu mija)
subtitle: Master stem-final consonant shifts in noun declensions and past-tense verbs
keyPoint: Historical palatalization alters root-final consonants before front endings in 2nd declension genitives and 1st conjugation past tenses.

examples.en: Mežā mēs redzējām daudz zaļu egļu.
Tā ir mana vecākā brāļa istaba.

mistakes.note: Second declension nouns ending in '-is' mutate their final stem consonant in genitive singular (l -> ļ): brālis -> brāļa.
Stem 'z' mutates into 'ž' (nazis -> naža), not into 'zj' or other unassimilated clusters.
Female nouns in the 5th declension mutate 'zn' to 'žņ' in the genitive plural (zvaigzne -> zvaigžņu).

quiz.question: What is the genitive singular form of 'lācis' (bear)?
quiz.explanation: In 2nd declension genitive singular, 'c' undergoes consonant mutation into 'č', yielding 'lāča'.

quiz.question: What is the genitive singular form of 'skapis' (cupboard)?
quiz.explanation: Labial consonants (b, p, m, v) append 'j' upon palatalization: 'p' becomes 'pj', making 'skapja'.

quiz.question: What is the genitive plural of the 5th declension feminine noun 'krūze' (mug)?
quiz.explanation: In 5th declension genitive plural, 'z' mutates into 'ž', giving 'krūžu'.

quiz.question: Which shift accurately reflects the consonant mutation rule in Latvian?
quiz.explanation: The liquid 'l' consistently mutates to palatal lateral 'ļ' (e.g., brālis -> brāļa). Note that 't' mutates to 'š', not 'č'.

tip: Labials (p, b, m, v) never soften alone; they simply insert a 'j' directly after them (p > pj, b > bj, m > mj, v > vj).

title: Definite vs. Indefinite Adjective Endings
subtitle: Choose endings (-s/-a vs. -ais/-ā) to specify definiteness and familiarity
keyPoint: Use indefinite endings (-s/-a) for new or non-specific items, and definite endings (-ais/-ā) after demonstratives, possessives, or for unique referents.

cells: šis jaunais auto / tā vecā skola

useCases.label: Geographic Names and Terms
useCases.example: Baltijas jūra ir auksta un skaista.

examples.en: Rīgā ir vecs un skaists tornis.
Šis jaunais kaimiņš ir ļoti draudzīgs.

mistakes.note: Demonstrative pronouns like 'šis' (this) or 'tas' (that) force any modifying adjective to take the definite ending ('jaunais').
Vocatives and direct address require the definite adjective declension ('dārgie draugi').

mistakes.wrong: Klusais okeāns ir liels okeāns, bet Melns jūra ir mazāka.
mistakes.note: Proper geographic designations (the Black Sea, the Baltic Sea) always require definite endings ('Melnā jūra').

quiz.question: Choose the correct form: 'Mums ir ___ dārzs.' (We have a large garden.)
quiz.explanation: Introducing an unspecified item for the first time without demonstratives calls for the indefinite masculine ending '-s' ('liels').

quiz.question: Choose the correct form: 'Kur ir ___ atslēga?' (Where is the green key? [specific known key])
quiz.explanation: The reference is to a specific, identifiable key, requiring the feminine definite ending '-ā' ('zaļā').

quiz.question: Complete the phrase: 'Tas ___ puisis labi runā latviski.' (That young boy speaks Latvian well.)
quiz.explanation: The demonstrative pronoun 'tas' requires the accompanying adjective to take the definite masculine suffix '-ais'.

quiz.question: Which of the following phrases is correct for addressing a dear friend directly?
quiz.explanation: Forms of direct address (vocative context) strictly require definite adjective morphology ('Mīļais draugs!').

tip: Whenever you see 'mans' (my), 'tavs' (your), 'šis' (this), or 'tas' (that) in front of an adjective, immediately default to the definite endings (-ais / -ā)!

title: Simple Past Tense Formation
subtitle: Conjugating verbs in the past across all three verb groups
keyPoint: The simple past tense adds the person endings (-u, -i, -a, -ām, -āt, -a) to the past stem, which often involves an internal vowel change or consonant shift in 1st conjugation verbs.

examples.en: Vai tu redzēji to skaisto filmu?

mistakes.wrong: Es vakar redzēju viņu un saku čau.
mistakes.right: Es vakar redzēju viņu un teicu čau.
mistakes.note: Maintain consistent past tense throughout; the past tense of 'teikt' (to say) is 'teicu', not present 'saku'.
Do not forget that prepositional destination phrases still govern their required case ('uz' takes accusative).
Direct objects in simple past sentences still require the accusative case ('ūdeni', not nominative 'ūdens').

quiz.question: Vakar mēs visu dienu ___ mājās.
quiz.explanation: The subject 'mēs' requires the 1st person plural past ending '-ām' (palikām).

quiz.question: Ko tu vakar vakarā ___?
quiz.explanation: The subject 'tu' requires the 2nd person singular past ending '-i' (darīji).

quiz.question: Kārlis pagājušajā gadā ___ uz Jelgavu.
quiz.explanation: Third-person singular reflexive past for 'pārcelties' uses the ending '-ās' (pārcēlās).

quiz.question: Es no rīta agri ___ kafiju.
quiz.explanation: The 1st person singular past of 'dzert' with internal vowel lengthening (e -> ē) is 'dzēru'.

tip: In the 3rd person (viņš, viņa, viņi, viņas), the ending is always identically '-a' (or '-ās' for reflexive) regardless of whether the subject is singular or plural!

title: Genitive Case for Possession, Quantities, and Negation
subtitle: Expressing ownership, amounts with adverbs, and absent items
keyPoint: In Latvian, the genitive case expresses possession (placed before the noun), follows adverbs of quantity like 'daudz' and 'maz', and replaces the nominative subject in negative existential sentences.

useCases.label: Adverbs of Measure
useCases.example: Veikalā ir maz piena un daudz ābolu.

examples.en: Man šobrīd diemžēl nav laika runāt.
Mums mājās nav maizes un piena.
Cik glāžu ūdens tu izdzer dienā?

mistakes.note: Negative existence ('nav') always demands genitive ('laika'), never nominative ('laiks').
In Latvian, the possessor in genitive comes before the possessed object, not after.
Adverbs of quantity like 'daudz' require genitive plural ('cilvēku'), not nominative plural ('cilvēki').

quiz.question: Šodien ārā ir ļoti daudz ___.
quiz.explanation: Quantity adverb 'daudz' requires the genitive singular form 'sniega'.

quiz.question: Mūsu pilsētā nav liela ___.
quiz.explanation: Negative existence with 'nav' requires masculine genitive singular '-a' (teātra).

quiz.question: Kur ir ___ soma?
quiz.explanation: Possession requires the genitive form placed first: 'māsas soma' (sister's bag).

quiz.question: Kafijā ir par daudz ___.
quiz.explanation: 'Daudz' requires the genitive case: 'cukura' (of sugar).

tip: Whenever you see 'nav' indicating something does not exist or isn't present, immediately switch the noun from nominative to genitive!

title: Verbal Prefixes and Aspectual Pairs
subtitle: Adding prefixes to specify direction, completion, and telicity
keyPoint: Attaching spatial prefixes like no-, iz-, aiz-, pie-, and uz- converts imperfective base verbs into perfective verbs signifying completed or directional action.

useCases.label: Full Completion (Telic)
useCases.example: Es beidzot izlasīju šo biezo grāmatu.

useCases.label: Arrival or Approach
useCases.example: Pienāc tuvāk un paskaties uz karti.

examples.en: Viņa ātri izdzēra glāzi auksta ūdens.

mistakes.wrong: Es lasīju grāmatu un tagad zinu beigas.
mistakes.right: Es izlasīju grāmatu un tagad zinu beigas.
mistakes.note: Use 'izlasīt' (prefixed perfective) when the entire book has been read from start to finish.
Use prefix 'at-' for motion arriving towards the speaker; 'aiz-' indicates movement away.
'Nopirkt' means to purchase an item, while 'uzpirkt' means to bribe someone or buy up stock.

quiz.question: Vai tu jau esi ___ visu šo rakstu?
quiz.explanation: 'Izlasīt' denotes reading a text to completion.

quiz.question: Lūdzu, ___ pie manis rīt pusdienlaikā.
quiz.explanation: 'Atnākt' means to come/arrive toward the speaker's location.

quiz.question: Autobuss tikko ___ no pieturas.
quiz.explanation: The prefix 'aiz-' designates departure/moving away from a location.

quiz.question: Es gribu ___ vēstuli vecmāmiņai.
quiz.explanation: 'Uzrakstīt' is the standard perfective counterpart for composing a letter or message.

tip: Base verbs in Latvian naturally focus on the ongoing process, while adding a prefix shifts the focus decisively to the end result or specific spatial trajectory.

title: Reflexive Verbs and Suffixation (-ties)
subtitle: Navigating reflexive endings across tenses and reciprocal semantics
keyPoint: Reflexive verbs end in -ties in the infinitive and take specialized personal endings containing -o-, -ie-, or -ā- instead of the regular active verb suffixes.

useCases.label: Self-Directed Actions
useCases.example: No rīta es ātri saģērbjos un nomazgājos.

examples.en: Mēs priecājamies par taviem labajiem panākumiem.
Cikos tu parasti mosties no rītiem?

mistakes.wrong: Es mācu latviešu valodu skolā (when meaning 'I study').
mistakes.note: 'Mācīt' means to teach someone else; 'mācīties' (reflexive) means to study/learn oneself.
Reciprocal meetings require the reflexive form 'satikties' (mēs satiekamies), not transitive active 'satikt'.
'Baidīties' is an inherently reflexive verb requiring the reflexive ending '-ās'.

quiz.question: Mēs katru svētdienu ___ ar veciem draugiem.
quiz.explanation: The reciprocal action 'to meet each other' requires reflexive 1st person plural 'tiekamies'.

quiz.question: Vai tu rīt ___ uz teātri?
quiz.explanation: The 2nd person singular future reflexive ending is '-sies' (pucēsies).

quiz.question: Es vakar ļoti vēlu ___.
quiz.explanation: 1st person singular past of reflexive 'aizmigt' (active conjugation with reflexive nuance) or standard root past is 'aizmigu'.

quiz.question: Viņi vienmēr ___ par jaunumiem.
quiz.explanation: 3rd person (singular & plural) present reflexive ending is '-as' / '-ās' (interesējas).

tip: Notice that in the future tense of reflexive verbs, the 2nd person singular ('tu') and 3rd person ('viņš/viņa/viņi') share the identical ending: '-sies'!

title: Declinable Active and Passive Participles
subtitle: Forming verbal adjectives in -ošs, -is/-usi, -ts, and -ams/-āms
keyPoint: Declinable participles act as verbal adjectives, agreeing in gender, number, and case with the nouns they modify while encoding active or passive voice and tense.

useCases.label: Passive Completed State
useCases.example: Šis nams ir uzcelts pagājušajā gadsimtā.

examples.en: Ezerā peld runājoši un smaidoši jaunieši.
Visi logi šajā vecajā ēkā bija aizvērti.

mistakes.note: Participles are declinable adjectives; they must match the accusative case of the direct object ('dziedošu meiteni').
Latvian avoids using 'no + Genitive' for agents in passive constructions; use active perfect participles instead.
When functioning as an attributive definite descriptor, use the definite participle ending ('-ais / -usī').

quiz.question: Pie loga sēdēja zēns, ___ interesantu grāmatu.
quiz.explanation: The masculine nominative singular present active participle modifying 'zēns' is 'lasošs'.

quiz.question: Šie dokumenti jau ir ___ vakar.
quiz.explanation: Passive past participle modifying masculine plural nominative 'dokumenti' takes the ending '-ti' (parakstīti).

quiz.question: Meitene, ___ uz Rīgu, jutās priecīga.
quiz.explanation: Feminine nominative singular active past participle takes '-usi' (aizbraukusi).

quiz.question: Tas ir visiem viegli ___ jautājums.
quiz.explanation: Present passive participle modifying masculine nominative singular 'jautājums' is 'saprotams' (understandable).

tip: Active past participles (-is/-usi) combined with forms of 'būt' build Latvian's compound tenses like the Present Perfect (esmu redzējis) and Past Perfect (biju aizgājis)!

title: Compound Past and Perfect Tenses
subtitle: Combining auxiliary 'būt' with active participles to show completed results
keyPoint: Form compound perfect tenses by combining the conjugated auxiliary verb 'būt' with past active participles ending in -is/-usi (singular) or -uši/-ušas (plural) matching the subject's gender and number.

useCases.label: Action completed before another past event
useCases.example: Kad viņš zvanīja, mēs jau bijām izgājuši.

useCases.label: Action to be finished before a future point
useCases.example: Rīt līdz trijiem es būšu pabeidzis darbu.

examples.en: Anna jau ir aizbraukusi uz Rīgu.
Vai tu esi kādreiz bijis Liepājā?
Līdz vakaram viņš būs izlasījis šo grāmatu.

mistakes.note: The participle must agree in gender and number with the feminine singular subject.
Plural masculine subjects require the plural ending -uši instead of the singular -is.

mistakes.wrong: Es esmu dzīvojis šeit divus gadus tagad.
mistakes.right: Es šeit dzīvoju jau divus gadus.
mistakes.note: Use simple present for ongoing actions starting in the past and continuing into the present; compound perfect marks completed actions.

quiz.question: Kad mēs atnācām, viņa jau ___ mājās.
quiz.explanation: The past perfect feminine singular requires 'bija' paired with 'aizgājusi'.

quiz.question: Kāpēc tu vēl neesi ___ šo uzdevumu?
quiz.explanation: Present perfect addressing a female singular speaker uses 'neesi' followed by the feminine participle 'pabeigusi'.

quiz.question: Līdz rītdienai zēni jau ___ visu nepieciešamo.
quiz.explanation: Future perfect with a masculine plural subject takes 'būs' and 'nopirkuši'.

quiz.question: Mēs (females) ___ ļoti nogurušas pēc ceļa.
quiz.explanation: First-person plural feminine past perfect requires 'bijām' plus 'bijušas'.

tip: Remember that 3rd person auxiliary 'ir' and 'bija' stay invariant whether the subject is singular or plural; only the participle changes its ending (-is, -usi, -uši, -ušas).

title: Conditional Mood (Vēlējuma izteiksme)
subtitle: Hypothetical wishes, politeness, and counterfactuals using -tu
keyPoint: Attach the invariant suffix -tu to the verb infinitive stem to form the simple conditional, or combine 'būtu' with active past participles to create past counterfactual conditionals.

useCases.label: Present hypothetical conditions
useCases.example: Ja man būtu laiks, es tev palīdzētu.

useCases.label: Unreal past counterfactuals
useCases.example: Ja tu būtu piezvanījis, es būtu atbraucis.

examples.en: Ja rīt spīdētu saule, mēs brauktu pie jūras.
Vai tu man palīdzētu ar šo somu?
Ja viņa būtu zinājusi patiesību, viņa nebūtu klusējusi.
Bērni ļoti priecātos par jaunu suni.

mistakes.wrong: Ja es būšu bagāts, es pirktu māju.
mistakes.right: Ja es būtu bagāts, es pirktu māju.
mistakes.note: In unreal/hypothetical conditional clauses, use the conditional 'būtu', not the future indicative 'būšu'.
Personal pronoun 'es' pairs with non-reflexive 'gribētu'. The reflexive 'gribētos' requires dative 'man gribētos'.

mistakes.wrong: Ja viņš atnāktu vakar, viss būtu labi.
mistakes.right: Ja viņš būtu atnācis vakar, viss būtu labi.
mistakes.note: Past counterfactual events require the compound conditional 'būtu atnācis', not the simple conditional 'atnāktu'.

quiz.question: Ja man būtu nauda, es noteikti ___ šo automašīnu.
quiz.explanation: Simple conditional requires the suffix '-tu' (nopirktu) to match the hypothetical 'ja man būtu'.

quiz.question: Vai jūs ___ lūdzu man padot sāli?
quiz.explanation: 'Varētu' expresses a polite present request ('Could you please pass...').

quiz.question: Ja mēs vakar nebūtu aizgulējušies, mēs ___ vilcienu.
quiz.explanation: Past unreal conditional in the main clause uses 'nebūtu' + past participle 'nokavējuši'.

quiz.question: Viņi noteikti ___ par taviem panākumiem.
quiz.explanation: Reflexive verbs take the conditional ending '-tos' (priecāties -> priecātos).

tip: Unlike indicative tenses, the simple conditional '-tu' never inflects for person or number: 'es ietu', 'tu ietu', 'viņš ietu', 'mēs ietu' all take the exact same suffix!

title: Indeclinable Adverbial Participles (-ot, -oties, -dam-)
subtitle: Connecting simultaneous actions with semi-predicative participle forms
keyPoint: Use indeclinable -ot/-oties when an adverbial action is concurrent with the main verb, and inflected semi-predicative -dams/-dama to emphasize simultaneous actions sharing the exact same grammatical subject.

examples.en: Ejot uz darbu, es satiku vecu draugu.
Domādams par nākotni, viņš pieņēma lēmumu.

mistakes.note: Dziedāt is non-reflexive; for a feminine subject performing simultaneous action, use 'dziedādama' or indeclinable 'dziedot'.
The semi-predicative participle must match masculine singular subject 'vīrietis' (-dams, not feminine -dama).

mistakes.right: Kad es iegāju istabā, gaisma ieslēdzās.
mistakes.note: Avoid dangling participles in -ot when the logical agent does not match or clearly relate to the subject, unless intended as dative absolute.

quiz.question: Māsa ___ iegāja savā istabā.
quiz.explanation: 'Māsa' is feminine singular, so the semi-predicative participle requires the ending '-dama'.

quiz.question: ___ ārā pa logu, mēs pamanījām pirmo sniegu.
quiz.explanation: The indeclinable reflexive adverbial participle in '-oties' (skatoties) describes the concurrent background action.

quiz.question: Vērotājs stāvēja klusēdams, neko ___ .
quiz.explanation: 'Nesakot' forms an indeclinable adverbial modifier ('without saying anything').

quiz.question: Draugi devās mājup, skaļi ___ par redzēto.
quiz.explanation: Masculine plural subject 'draugi' with a reflexive verb takes '-damies' (or alternatively indeclinable 'sarunājoties', but '-damies' specifically agrees with masculine plural).

tip: Distinguish -ot and -dams easily: -ot is completely indeclinable and never changes endings; -dams/-dama behaves like an adjective and must agree in gender and number with the subject.

title: Relative Mood / Evidentiality (Atstāstījuma izteiksme)
subtitle: Reporting hearsay, rumours, and secondhand claims without personal endorsement
keyPoint: Use the relative mood ending in -ot (present) or 'esot' + past participle (past) to report speech, unverified claims, or folklore where the speaker disclaims direct responsibility.

cells: They say it will rain heavily.

useCases.label: Indirect reported speech without 'ka'
useCases.example: Jānis teica: viņš šodien nevarot nākt.

useCases.label: Folkloric or legendary narration
useCases.example: Reiz senos laikos te esot dzīvojis milzis.

examples.en: Meteorologi brīdina, ka rīt būšot stipra vētra.
Kaimiņi stāsta, ka viņa esot pārdevusi savu dzīvokli.
Pēteris teica, ka viņš šodien strādājot no mājām.
Viņš apgalvo, ka neko par to nezinot.
Visi runā, ka direktors drīz iecelšot jaunu vadītāju.

mistakes.wrong: Viņa teica, ka viņa ir slima (when reporting doubt).
mistakes.right: Viņa teica, ka viņa esot slima.
mistakes.note: Using the indicative 'ir' indicates the speaker verifies it as fact; 'esot' signals secondhand attribution or non-verified speech.

mistakes.wrong: Viņš saka, ka rīt būs līst.
mistakes.note: Future relative uses the specific future stem suffix '-šot' (līt -> līšot), not 'būs līst'.

mistakes.wrong: Kāpēc tu saki, ka es negribu palīdzēt?
mistakes.right: Kāpēc tu saki, ka es negribot palīdzēt?
mistakes.note: When repeating an assertion someone else claims you made, standard Latvian uses relative mood 'negribot'.

quiz.question: Radio ziņo, ka rīt visā valstī ___ pirmais sniegs.
quiz.explanation: Future hearsay reported in news broadcasts uses the future relative ending '-šot' (snigšot).

quiz.question: Draugs apgalvo, ka viņš nekad ___ šo cilvēku.
quiz.explanation: Past reported assertion uses the relative auxiliary 'neesot' followed by the past participle 'redzējis'.

quiz.question: Māte stāsta, ka mazais brālis jau brīvi ___ angliski.
quiz.explanation: Present reported speech without the speaker's direct observation takes the present relative '-ot' (runājot).

quiz.question: Leģenda vēsta, ka šajā pilī reiz ___ noslēpumaina princese.
quiz.explanation: Traditional legends reporting past events take 'esot' + feminine participle 'dzīvojusi'.

tip: Think of the relative mood as built-in quotation marks: replacing 'iet' with 'ejot' or 'būs' with 'būšot' grammatically tells the listener 'someone told me this, but don't hold me to it!'

title: Dative Absolute Construction (Datīva absolūts)
subtitle: Independent subordinate clauses with dative subjects and -ot participles
keyPoint: The Dative Absolute (datīva absolūts) pairs an independent subject in the dative case with an adverbial participle ending in -ot or -oties to build a concise temporal, causal, or concessive subordinate clause.

useCases.label: Causal circumstance ('because / as')
useCases.example: Tēvam saslimstot, dēlam nācās pārņemt darbu.

useCases.label: Concessive circumstance ('even though')
useCases.example: Lietum līstot, mēs tomēr devāmies pārgājienā.

examples.en: Saulei lecot, putni sāka skaļi dziedāt.
Mācību gadam beidzoties, skolēni devās brīvdienās.
Pulkstenim sitot divpadsmit, visi pacēla glāzes.
Tumsai iestājoties, pilsētas ielās iedegās laternas.

mistakes.note: The subject of an absolute participle clause must be in the dative case ('saulei'), never the nominative ('saule').

mistakes.wrong: Man ejot uz mājām, es satiku Jāni.
mistakes.right: Ejot uz mājām, es satiku Jāni.
mistakes.note: If the subordinate clause subject and the main clause subject are identical ('es'), use a simple adverbial participle (-ot or -dams), not the dative absolute.

mistakes.right: Kamēr pūta vējš, bērni pūta balonus.
mistakes.note: While grammatically valid, avoid using dative absolute when subjects can easily cause semantic ambiguity with the main action verbs.

quiz.question: ___ rietot, debesis kļuva koši sarkanas.
quiz.explanation: The dative absolute construction strictly demands the dative case for its independent subject ('saulei').

quiz.question: Mācībām ___, visi bērni izskrēja pagalmā.
quiz.explanation: The reflexive participle ending '-oties' (beidzoties) combines with dative 'mācībām' to mark simultaneous completion.

quiz.question: Lietum ___, mēs tomēr nolēmām palikt mežā.
quiz.explanation: The indeclinable participle suffix '-ot' (līstot) forms the predicate of the dative absolute clause.

quiz.question: ___ ienākot zālē, visi piecēlās kājās.
quiz.explanation: Dative singular masculine 'prezidentam' is needed before participle 'ienākot'.

tip: Golden rule: never use a dative absolute if both clauses share the same subject! Use 'Es ejot satiku...' ONLY if someone else is doing the meeting; if you met him yourself, write 'Ejot mājās, es satiku...'.
